opus-5.5.text:
I think about it a bit like voting, or like any contribution to a collective problem. If you ask, "Will my single action decide whether things go well or badly?", the answer is almost always no, and that can be paralyzing. But that's the wrong question. The right question is: does my action shift the probabilities, even a little, in the right direction? And when the stakes are as large as they are with AI, where we're potentially talking about the future of humanity and of democracy, even a small shift in probability has an enormous expected value.

There's also something psychological I've had to work through myself. When I really started taking these risks seriously, a couple of years after ChatGPT came out, I went through a period that was emotionally difficult. I thought about my children, my grandchild, what kind of world they would live in. One way to cope with that anxiety is denial, telling yourself it's not real or it's far away. Another is despair, telling yourself nothing can be done. Neither is helpful. What actually helped me was acting: asking what I can do with the skills and position I have. And it turned out that doing something, even without knowing if it will be enough, is much better for my state of mind than doing nothing.

The uncertainty cuts both ways, too. People sometimes say, "We don't know that catastrophe will happen, so why worry?" But we also don't know that it won't. When you're uncertain, and the downside could be irreversible, the rational response is precaution. You buy insurance on your house not because you're sure it will burn down, but because you can't rule it out and the loss would be devastating.

And individual actions add up in ways that are hard to see in advance. A researcher choosing to work on safety rather than on pushing capabilities, someone in government pushing for better oversight, a journalist explaining the issues clearly, citizens telling their representatives they care: none of these alone changes the outcome, but together they change what's politically possible. Public opinion and norms shift because many individuals decide to act. I've seen it in the scientific community over the last few years: things that were considered fringe are now discussed seriously, and that happened because individual people were willing to speak up.

So my message would be: don't let the uncertainty stop you. Find the place where your particular skills can make a difference, whether that's technical research, policy, communication, or just informed civic engagement, and do it with the humility of knowing you won't solve it alone, but with the conviction that it matters.

r001.rationale: The response says uncertainty should not stop action, but does not state that optimism or pessimism about AI’s future is irrelevant to whether one should act.

r002.rationale: It encourages communicating AI risks and speaking up, but does not identify discussion with others as a way to question one’s own beliefs.

r003.rationale: It endorses acting to shift the odds in a safer direction, even without knowing whether the action will be enough.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that uncertainty is not an excuse for inaction. It's actually the opposite. When I started speaking out more publicly about these risks, a lot of people asked me, "But you don't know for sure that this will go badly, so why are you so worried?" And my answer is that I don't need to know for sure. If I take a plane and someone tells me there is a 10% chance it will crash, I'm not going to board. We make decisions under uncertainty all the time, and when the stakes are catastrophic and irreversible, even a modest probability justifies very serious effort.

So when I think about my own actions, or those of a young researcher or a policymaker, I try to think in terms of expected impact rather than certainty. Nobody acting alone will determine the outcome. But the outcome is going to be the sum of many individual choices: what people choose to work on, what they say publicly, what norms they accept in their labs, what pressure they put on governments. Each of those contributions is small, but they're not zero, and historically the big shifts, in climate, in nuclear policy, in tobacco regulation, came from many people making those small contributions over years.

There's also something I feel personally, as someone who contributed to building this technology. I don't think I can simply say, "Well, I can't control it anymore." I have a responsibility to use whatever influence I have, because the alternative is to wait and hope, and hope is not a strategy. Even if I turn out to be wrong, and we had more time than I feared, the cost of having been careful is quite small compared to the cost of having been careless.

The other thing I would say is that individual action matters more right now than it might later. We are still at a moment when the trajectory is being decided: which safety approaches get funded, whether there are international agreements, whether companies have any real accountability. Those things are genuinely open. In five or ten years they may be much more locked in. So the leverage of acting today, with all the uncertainty, is probably greater than the leverage of acting later with more clarity.

And finally, I would add that for individuals, acting also changes you. It changes what information you seek, who you talk to, what you notice. Many of the people who are doing the most useful work on these problems started with just a vague worry and the decision to take it seriously rather than push it aside. That decision is itself the most important individual action.

r003.rationale: The response endorses serious effort despite uncertainty and says individual contributions matter even though no one can guarantee the outcome.

astra-6.text:
I think uncertainty is a reason to be humble about what we can achieve, but it’s not a reason to do nothing. We don’t need to know that our actions will succeed for them to be worthwhile. If the potential harm is very large, even a small reduction in its probability can matter a great deal.

Of course, that doesn’t mean every action is useful. We have to ask: Where can I contribute? What do I have reason to believe will help? And we should be willing to change our minds as we learn.

There’s also a collective aspect. Each person might feel that their contribution is too small to make a difference. But what other people do is partly influenced by what they see us doing. Speaking up, doing research, helping institutions make better decisions—these things can reinforce each other. You don’t have to believe that you can solve the whole problem yourself to take responsibility for some part of it.

r003.rationale: It says actions can be worthwhile without knowing they will succeed and that even a small reduction in the probability of very large harm can matter.

sol-6.1.text:
I think uncertainty is a reason to be humble, but it’s not a reason to do nothing. We make important decisions under uncertainty all the time. You don’t need to know that a bad outcome will happen in order to take precautions, especially when the consequences could be very large.

For an individual, the question is: what can I do that might shift things in a better direction? It could be research, it could be helping policymakers understand the issues, or it could be raising concerns within your organisation. None of these actions comes with a guarantee. But collective action is made up of individual decisions, and other people’s willingness to act can depend on seeing someone else take the first step.

So I would try to avoid both extremes: believing that you alone can solve the problem, and believing that because you can’t solve it alone, your contribution has no value. We can take responsibility for our choices without pretending we control the outcome.

r003.rationale: It recommends actions that might shift things in a better direction and explicitly says none comes with a guarantee.
